title: Nuclei and particles
tagline: From radioactive decay to the Standard Model
summary: Nuclear structure, decay, reactions, detectors, and the Standard Model of quarks and leptons.
overview: Nuclei and particles are quantum systems bound by interactions other than electromagnetism. A nucleus is a few hundred nucleons bound by the residual strong force; a hadron is a bound state of quarks; and the decays that power the Sun and that we detect in the laboratory are the weak interaction changing one fermion into another.

The course begins with nuclear sizes, the semi-empirical mass formula and the stability of nuclei, then the three modes of decay and the reactions of fission and fusion. Detectors and accelerators are treated as instruments with a principle, not as a catalogue. The second half is particle physics proper: the quark model, the leptons, and the gauge structure of the Standard Model at the level of its particles, its conservation laws and its one observed scalar, the Higgs boson.

Orders of magnitude matter here more than in any earlier course. A nuclear binding energy is a few MeV per nucleon, a rest energy is about a GeV per nucleon, and an atomic energy is an eV. Keeping those three numbers separate prevents most mistakes.
outcomes: Use the semi-empirical mass formula and interpret a binding-energy curve.
Compute lifetimes and spectra for alpha, beta and gamma decay in the standard approximations.
Describe fission and fusion in terms of the binding-energy curve and Q values.
Explain how a scintillator, a semiconductor detector and a tracking detector identify a particle.
State the quark content of the light hadrons and the conservation laws of the strong, electromagnetic and weak interactions.
Describe the particles of the Standard Model and the role of the Higgs boson.

history.title: Becquerel’s rays
history.detail: Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts darken a photographic plate wrapped against the light. Radioactivity was the first evidence of a nucleus with internal energy.

history.title: Rutherford’s nucleus
history.detail: The Geiger–Marsden scattering experiment, interpreted by Rutherford, showed that the positive charge of an atom sits in a region far smaller than the atom.

history.title: The neutron and the positron
history.detail: Chadwick identified the neutron. The same year Anderson observed the positron, the antiparticle Dirac had predicted.

history.title: Fermi’s theory of beta decay
history.detail: Fermi wrote a field theory of beta decay in which a neutron becomes a proton, an electron and a neutrino. It is the ancestor of the weak interaction.

history.title: Quarks
history.detail: Gell-Mann and, independently, Zweig proposed that hadrons are bound states of fractionally charged quarks. Deep inelastic scattering at SLAC, from 1968, showed the pointlike constituents.

history.title: The Higgs boson
history.detail: On 4 July 2012 the ATLAS and CMS collaborations at the LHC announced a boson near 125 GeV with the couplings expected of the Higgs boson of the Standard Model.
